Sample text:
---
# On Unfinished Things

There is a kind of comfort in leaving things unfinished. I don't mean the work that piles up and makes us anxious. I mean the half-read book face-down on the nightstand, the sweater with one sleeve knit and the other still on the needles, the letter that has been "almost done" for three weeks. These objects sit in our lives like open doors, and I have come to think they are some of the most honest things we own.

Finished things ask nothing of us. A completed painting hangs on the wall and tells you what it is. A novel, once you reach the last page, is closed for good, its ending fixed like a stone in a riverbed. That permanence has its own dignity, but it also has a kind of silence. Unfinished things keep talking. The unfinished sweater says, *you were once someone who wanted to make this for another person.* The bookmark says, *the story is still waiting, and so is the version of you who was enjoying it.*

I have a notebook filled with beginnings. Some are only a line long: a woman who keeps bees in a city apartment, a man who writes letters to a lighthouse keeper who died in 1911, a sentence about the smell of wet pennies that I wrote on a train and have never been able to continue. When I flip through it, I feel no shame at the abandoned pages. Instead I feel a strange sort of company. Each beginning is a small argument I once had with the world, and I am glad that some of those arguments were never settled, because an unsettled argument leaves room for later.

We live in a culture that prizes completion. We measure ourselves by output, by the number of projects shipped and goals crossed off. There is a particular modern anxiety in seeing a list with too many open items, as though each one were a debt. But I suspect much of what makes a life rich is precisely the amount of it that remains open. A person who has finished everything has, in a sense, run out of reasons to continue. The unfinished is the reserve, the place where curiosity lives.

Consider how gardens work. A garden is never finished. Even the most meticulous gardener is always in the middle of something: pruning, planting, waiting for the clematis to climb the fence it hasn't yet reached. The garden is valuable precisely because it is in process, because each season revises the last. Nobody walks through a garden and wishes it were complete. We walk through it wanting to see what it becomes.

Relationships work this way too. The best conversations with old friends never fully conclude. You pick up a thread from a decade ago and find it still tugging at something in both of you. Marriages that last are rarely built on a single moment of resolution; they are built on a thousand small continuations, on the daily decision to keep going with someone whose story is still being written. To finish a person, to decide you understand them entirely, is to close a door that should have stayed ajar.

Of course, there is a flip side. Some unfinished things are simply abandoned, and abandonment is not the same as openness. The unpaid bill, the apology never offered, the dream we stopped feeding because it felt too hard: these carry weight, and pretending otherwise is a kind of self-deception. The task, I think, is to learn the difference between what is waiting and what is wilting. A waiting thing still gets a glance now and then, still tugs at the attention. A wilting thing has become a reproach, and maybe the honest move is to let it go with some gratitude for what it taught.

I try, lately, to keep a few things deliberately open. I leave a chapter of a book unread for a month. I start a drawing I know I won't finish this week. I let the question stay a question instead of rushing it toward an answer. This feels less like laziness than like keeping faith with the possibility that I will be different later, that the person who returns to the sweater in spring will have learned something the person who began it did not.

There is also humility in the unfinished. It admits that we don't know how things will turn out, that our understanding is provisional, that the next page might change everything we thought we knew about the story. A finished life, if such a thing exists, is available only in retrospect, and even then only to others. From the inside, we are always mid-sentence.

So I have made a small peace with my clutter of incomplete things. The stacked books, the half-written letters, the seedlings that never quite became plants: they are evidence that I kept wanting things, kept starting, kept believing there would be time. That belief, however often it has been tested, seems to me one of the more hopeful habits a person can have.

Tonight I will probably not finish the book on my nightstand. I will read a few pages, put it face-down again, and turn off the lamp. In the morning it will still be there, open at the same place, waiting for me to come back and see what happens next. I find I am grateful for that. Some doors should stay open a little longer.
---
